summary: Updates RFC 5492 by changing the registration procedures for BGP Capability Codes. The former Private Use range is divided into First Come First Served, Experimental Use and Reserved ranges.

plainLanguage.summary: BGP peers use Capability Codes to identify optional protocol extensions. This RFC replaces the Private Use label for codes 128-255 with registration rules for shared, experimental, and reserved values.

questions: how are bgp capability codes registered
what changed in bgp capability code ranges
what ranges did rfc 8810 assign to bgp capability codes
subtitle: BGP Capability Codes 128-255 are reassigned among three registration ranges.

tldr.problem: RFC 5492 marked Capability Codes 128-255 as Private Use, a designation later found confusing to implementors.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8810 assigns 128-238 to First Come First Served, 239-254 to Experimental Use, and 255 as Reserved.
tldr.outcome: The full First Come First Served range is now 64-238, and the IETF controls future registrations.

today: RFC 8810 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5492. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The New Code Ranges
sections.content:
BGP peers use Capability Advertisement to tell one another about optional protocol extensions. Each extension is signaled with a Capability Code. RFC 5492 designated codes 128-255 for Private Use, which experience showed was confusing.

RFC 8810 revises that range: 128-238 is First Come First Served, 239-254 is Experimental Use, and 255 is Reserved. The ranges 1-63 (IETF Review) and 64-127 (First Come First Served) remain unchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: Some BGP code values now have clearer rules for how they are assigned. Codes 64 through 238 use First Come First Served registration, and the upper values are experimental or reserved.

sections.title: Why Experimental and Reserved Values
sections.content:
The Experimental Use range is intended for early development, not long-term use or shipping products. The RFC says this label reduces use of the scarce code space and that reclassifying the range later should be considered difficult.

Code 255 is reserved because it may be useful if the number space needs to be extended. A survey beginning August 14, 2015 gathered known uses of the former Private Use range, but the RFC says it cannot guarantee that every use was found.
sections.plainLanguage: Experimental values are for development rather than long-term products. The highest value is kept available in case the code space needs to grow.

sections.title: IANA Registry Changes
sections.content:
IANA revised the Capability Codes registry: 1-63 requires IETF Review, 64-238 uses First Come First Served, and 239-254 is Experimental Use. The IETF is the change controller for all future registrations.

IANA also recorded several deprecated prestandard uses at values 128-131 and 184-185, and marked 255 Reserved.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA updated the registry with the new ranges and recorded several earlier uses as deprecated. The IETF controls future registrations.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This revision to registration procedures does not change the underlying security issues in RFC 5492 or RFC 4271.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing the registration rules does not change the security issues described in the BGP specifications.
